claims.text: Local lattice distortion generated by atomic size mismatch is the dominant factor governing strength and deformation or failure behavior in multi-component concentrated alloys.
Greater atomic size mismatch among principal elements generates greater local lattice distortion.
Local lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion caused by lattice distortion raises yield strength.
Greater lattice distortion promotes a transition from homogeneous plasticity to localized strain.
Severe restriction of dislocation motion can cause deformation behavior to transition from ductile to brittle failure.
Atomic size mismatch produces heterogeneous lattice distortions that create energy barriers for dislocation glide.
Alloys with high lattice distortion will have higher yield strength than baseline alloys with minimal atomic size mismatch.
Alloys with high lattice distortion will have lower ductility than baseline alloys with minimal atomic size mismatch.
Alloys with high lattice distortion will show earlier strain localization or crack initiation than the baseline alloys.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily to single-phase alloys when dislocation glide is the principal mode of plasticity.
Below approximately 0.6 times the melting temperature, dislocation-mediated plasticity is expected to dominate under the proposed test conditions.
Near the melting temperature, diffusion-controlled processes may override the lattice-distortion mechanism.
Significant precipitation or secondary phases may override or obscure the lattice-distortion mechanism.
The magnitude and spatial distribution of local lattice distortion can be characterized using X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy.
Chemical short-range order, solute drag, and stacking-fault-energy variations may also contribute to the observed mechanical behavior.
